status_summary: DHS proposed a new public charge rule on 2025-11-19 and published the final rule on 2026-07-20, effective 2026-09-18, after 8,846 comments; it finalized the proposal substantially as proposed. The rule rescinds the 2022 public charge regulations and does not replace them with a regulatory definition; officers weigh the statutory factors case by case and, from the effective date, consider receipt of any means-tested public benefit, where before they considered only cash assistance and long-term institutional care. The rule also revises public charge bond rules so that receiving a means-tested benefit breaches a bond. DHS estimates about $13.05 billion a year in reduced transfer payments, with stated uncertainty. On 2026-09-14 New York's attorney general, with other states and DC, sued in the Southern District of New York, and a coalition of cities and counties filed a separate suit in the same court. A report dated 2026-09-18 says Judge Ronnie Abrams set an initial conference for 2026-10-09 in one of the cases; the filing-date releases from the New York attorney general and New York City, and that report, name no court order blocking the rule, no ruling and no preliminary-injunction motion. The design differs from the Mandate's reference to the first-term rule, so the match is parallel.

timeline.event: DHS publishes a proposed rule on the public charge ground of inadmissibility (90 FR 52168); comments closed 2025-12-19.

DHS publishes the final rule (91 FR 45324), effective 2026-09-18: it rescinds the 2022 regulations without a replacement definition, moves to case-by-case discretion that counts any means-tested benefit for applications on or after the effective date, and revises public charge bond rules; DHS received 8,846 comments and finalized the rule substantially as proposed.
USCIS issues updated policy guidance on how officers will apply the new standard, per an immigration-services blog.

State of New York et al. v. DHS is filed in the Southern District of New York by New York's attorney general with 21 other states and DC, and a coalition of cities and counties files a separate suit, arguing DHS exceeded its statutory authority; the report, dated 2026-09-18, says no court had blocked or delayed the rule at that point.

Massachusetts' attorney general announces that a multistate coalition filed suit in the Southern District of New York asking the court to declare the 2026 public charge rule unlawful and vacate it; the release names no preliminary injunction motion and no ruling.

New York's attorney general announces the suit in the Southern District of New York with other states and DC (the release counts 21 other states, lists 20 states and DC, and also names Pennsylvania's governor), asking the court to declare the 2026 rule unlawful and vacate it; the release names no preliminary-injunction motion and no ruling.

New York City announces a separate suit in the Southern District of New York by New York City, Chicago, San Francisco, Santa Clara County, Seattle, King County and the Public Rights Project, filed before the rule's expected 2026-09-18 effective date; the release names no court order or motion.

The rule takes effect for admission applications made, and adjustment applications filed or postmarked, on or after this date; applications before it are judged under the 2022 rule as to benefits received earlier.

A news report published on the effective date says the rule took effect with no court order blocking it, that both suits (22 states and DC; six cities and counties) are in the Southern District of New York, and that Judge Ronnie Abrams set an initial conference for 2026-10-09 in one of them.
